Ask of any proposed change or innovation: What will this do to our community? How will this affect our common wealth?

– Wendell Berry

Artwork by Natalie Shilo

 

Hello discoverers!

I don’t intend for DD to turn into another op-ed column chasing the week’s AI headlines, but if you’ve read the last few issues, you’ll have noticed I keep circling the same question: what kind of power is being built around these tools, and what can the rest of us do about it?

So the title of Garrett Bucks’ recent essay got my attention: The opposite of the apocalypse is a neighborhood

Bucks expresses something that goes through my head whenever I hear one of these CEOs talking nonchalantly about the likelihood of the end times:

“If I were an executive at a company that produced water guzzling theft machines, and I also believed that there was more than a 10% chance that my robots would kill us all, I’d like to think that I’d offer more than vague gestures of concern.”

Like Bucks, I think the apocalypse talk is overcooked. The more pressing worry is the one Bucks borrows from Tressie McMillan Cottom: that AI is just one visible part of “a superstructure that merges regressive politics with unchecked economic power in the guise of technological innovation”.

Gary Marcus makes a similar point in another recent essay. Extinction isn’t what keeps him up at night. Wars escalated by AI-generated disinformation and hacks on critical infrastructure do.

“My p(doom) is low; my p(dystopia) is high.”

A handful of men rewriting the rules of the economy and geopolitics out of greed and a hunger for power makes for a duller plot than killer robots. It’s still plenty dangerous.

I share Bucks’ anger about the way tech sneaks into every crevice of our lives without us always noticing (or noticing too late) what we give up in return.

“I’m mad at myself for all the previous times I’ve been conned, when I thought that past technological breakthroughs actually would make my life better, when I excused somebody else’s love of wealth and power because my phone got cooler and played more songs on demand.”

Don’t look for much practical advice in his essay. It’s more like a love letter to being human.

“When everything that makes you human is outsourced to a big, dumb beep boop machine, the only logical responses is to revel in the absolute best parts of our humanity, loudly and collectively.”

“And that is enough, at least in aggregate, at least with persistence and organization and threads being tied between one community’s fight against a data center and another town’s valiant stand for all of our kids’ future.”

I’m hardly a purist here. I have a skeleton Facebook account for Marketplace sales, I still collaborate in Google Docs, and yes, I lean on the odd AI tool when a job is tedious enough.

Most of us are tangled up in these systems in one way or another – let’s not pretend otherwise. But being implicated doesn’t disqualify us from calling them out, in the same way you can drive a car and still argue for cities built around walking/cycling.

The difficult part is making sure the convenience doesn’t end up making our decisions. So it’s worth pausing to ask what we actually want from a human life, and whether the tools we reach for each day are bringing us closer to it or talking us out of it.

“We don’t need the robots. We never did. We need to be less alone, and less vulnerable to the whims of billionaires. We need our towns and neighborhoods to be celebrated, to feel like where we live and who we are matters. We need neighbors who pick up the slack when we reach the limit of our abilities and energy.”

“It isn’t just that we don’t want to die. It’s that we want to live, and we don’t want to do it alone.”

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

Sponsor

Your feed used to be your friends.

Now it’s ads, strangers, and whatever keeps you scrolling. boopr is that feed again: the people you actually know, their newest posts first. That’s it.

Open it, catch up, message a friend, maybe send a boop (a photo for one person, gone once they’ve seen it). A session takes about 30 seconds.

There’s no Discover tab and no public profiles. You add friends in person or with a code, so the feed reads like a group chat: real life, not content.

Only you and your friends can see what you share. No ads, ever. boopr is funded by an optional subscription, not by selling your attention.

Free on iOS and Android. No email or phone number to sign up.

Tools

Gravity

One-stream notes app

Built around an ‘append-and-review’ method, Gravity is a note-taking app with a single, endless stream instead of folders and tags. New thoughts go on top, old ones sink as you add more, and a swipe bumps anything still relevant back up. Local-first with optional iCloud sync, on iOS, macOS and Android, and no subscription.

Activate Fitness

Steps buy you screen time

An activity app that makes kids move to unlock other apps. Parents can set activity goals and app restrictions on a paired iPhone, along with lockout times for school and bedtime, and bonus minutes for things like chores or good grades. I’m not entirely sold on turning exercise and good behaviour into a points system and using more apps to solve our screen problem, but I can see why some parents might find it useful.

Atlas

Mac moodboard app

If you hoard reference images, Atlas keeps them in ordinary folders on your own Mac (or your cloud drive) and lets you browse them as a grid, push them around on a canvas, or drift through an endless ‘Infinity’ view. For saving, use their browser extension or the menu bar drop target. And it’s a one-time fee. Friends of DD enjoy a 20% discount. Become a Friend to access specials like this.

Control Panel for YouTube

Make YouTube behave again

Block ads, hide Shorts and AI summaries, switch off Autoplay, related videos and the Home feed entirely. This browser extension “gives you more control over YouTube by adding missing options and UI improvements”. There’s a long tail of smaller fixes too – hiding watched videos past a percentage you set, muting whole channels, restoring bits of the old player UI. There is even a mobile version.

Wanderings

Charming discoveries from the internet’s back alleys that you don’t need but might love.

Corporate Lobbying

A tool that scrapes the lobbying disclosures US companies are legally required to file and maps them to stock tickers. You can search by company or keyword and see who’s paying what to influence which bills.

ChipTycoon

A little isometric chip factory where you watch a single wafer going through all twenty-two stages of chipmaking – sand to rough silicon to a mirror-flat disc, then coated, printed, etched and wired layer by layer.

Council Spend Map

A project that pulls together the payment data English councils are required to publish and puts it on a searchable map. You can poke around by council, supplier, category or year and see who’s actually getting public money.

Legal Graffiti Walls

A community-maintained directory of legal graffiti walls worldwide, with some 2,590 spots mapped across 70-odd countries – halls of fame, underpasses, even Antarctica!

Techno Optimism Archive

This will have to grow a lot to cover the last two decades: an archive of newspaper clippings and posts from the moments when a new invention was going to fix everything – and then didn’t.
 

Books

The Creatures’ Guide to Caring

Why we’re built to care

From frog dads carrying tadpoles on their backs to orca grandmothers hunting to feed their grown sons – science journalist Elizabeth Preston goes deep on how caretaking evolved, and what we can learn from it. With warmth and humour, she discovers (unsurprisingly) that humans were never meant to raise children alone: we evolved to do it in cooperative groups.

Living Democracy

Rethinking democracy together

Environmentalist and community activist Tim Hollo makes the case for a more participatory form of democracy as a way through the climate crisis, inequality and social division. Drawing on ecological thinking, First Nations knowledge and community action, it’s an optimistic argument for building a future based on mutual aid and collective problem-solving.

Media

The opposite of the apocalypse is a neighborhood

Read

This piece is a lovely little reminder to keep fighting for what makes us human. Garrett Bucks argues that the real threat of AI isn’t extinction, but a ‘malevolent superstructure’ that merges regressive politics with unchecked economic power and human condescension. Instead of despair, we ought to resist by fiercely celebrating our humanity and building interconnected local communities.

“Call it conspiracy theorizing or savvy cynicism, but when the foxes hold a press conference about how the hens should do more to regulate them, there’s cause for wariness.”

How To Give Everyday People A Say In AI Governance

Read

If the previous DD issue made you wonder how people can be more involved in the rules around AI, this piece offers an ambitious framework for doing that. Yes, it may sound like wishful thinking given how the broligarchy currently gatekeeps the tech, but leveraging the massive scale of existing AI platforms to consult billions of people is a solution that uniquely suits the tech itself.

“Doomism and competitiveness anxiety are terrible organizing principles. ... Whether the danger is an AI slipping out of human hands or sovereignty slipping out of governments’ grasp, the fix is the same: More people, not fewer, need a say before consequential decisions are made.”

Fold Laundry With Me!

Read

Today’s hyper-curated homes and isolated self-care have made us treat our living spaces like private fortresses. I really like Julie Beck’s encouragement to open our messy homes for more impromptu hangs with friends, instead of meticulously organised dinner parties. After all, lowering our standards of perfection and inviting people into our humility rather than our standard of excellence is what actually builds real closeness. (Paywalled – free archived view)

“In 2021, Mark Ellwood wrote for the luxury lifestyle magazine Robb Report about visitor-discouraging design choices the rich were making for their homes – things such as installing long driveways and eliminating doorbells. Ellwood diagnosed them with ‘Big House Small Welcome Syndrome.’”

The product of the railways is the timetable

Read

You’ll enjoy this if you’re into trains and transport engineering: Benedict Springbett argues that because train movements across a network are deeply interdependent, the product of the railways is the timetable, not individual tracks or trains. It sounds obvious, but only a few countries understand and execute this master plan well – like the Swiss.

“The possibility of an hour’s delay is just accepted as a fact of life on a road trip or a flight, whereas with railways, we start tutting as soon as the train is merely five minutes late. We become irritated because we hold the railways to a high standard of reliability, and we hold them to that standard because they generally fulfil it.”

Wealth Inequality in America (Updated 2026)

Watch

Thirteen years after the YouTube channel @politizane published an animated explainer on American wealth inequality that went viral, they are back with an update comparing how unequal people think the US is with how unequal it really is. We all know the numbers are grim, but the way they illustrate and explain them is still eye-opening.
 

Inspiration

The work by South Korean illustrator and painter Seong Ryul depicts sunny, slightly dreamlike landscapes and fragments from everyday life. They often show fleeting moments that disappear or change shape. Look at those cloud formations!

Combining art practices into a new medium I’ve never seen before: Nosheen Iqbal builds geometric reliefs from wooden panels, semi-precious beads and layered thread, drawing on her Pakistani heritage and the ornamental logic of Islamic architecture.

Font of the week: Nan Gothic is a warm, unpretentious take on the American gothics of the mid-20th century, keeping their quirks and sturdiness but adding sweeping tails on the /t and /y and 20° italics and backslants.

Numbers

80.2

After a scorching summer, air conditioner sales are up 80.2% year on year in Germany, with portable unit sales up 112.9%. Currently, less than 20% of German homes have air conditioning.

1.16

The number of public EV chargers in the EU has grown almost eightfold since 2020, reaching 1.16 million by June 2026, indicating that there are sufficient public chargers for the current EU fleet on the road.
